item.title: 24 Nov 2026
item.description:
To the land of no return, the land of darkness,
Ishtar, daughter of the Moon, directed her thought, [...]
To the house of shadows, the dwelling of Irkalla,
To the house without exit for him who enters therein,
To the road whence there is no turning,
To the house without light for him who enters therein,
The place where dust is their nourishment, clay their food.

(Descent of the Goddess Ishtar into the Lower World, as translated by Morris Jastrow, Jr.)

ὡς γὰρ
For such ἐπεκλώσαντο θεοὶ
have the gods spun δειλοῖσι βροτοῖσι
for wretched mortals:

ζώειν
to live ἀχνυμένοις:
grieving, αὐτοὶ δέ τ’
while they ἀκηδέες εἰσί.
are without a care!

(Akhilleus speaking. Homeros, Ilias XXIV 525–6.)

Our foolish society likes to rank everything in order, as if the world were one dimensional. Perhaps we even have Platon to blame for this, as his tendency to trace everything back to Absolute Good runs all through Western history, from Plotinos to Saint Anselm to Progressivism; but Platon’s “Good” is not necessarily what humans might think of as pleasant, and back when I was running a business, I always used to try and teach my employees that there’s no such thing as “better:” every upside has a downside, every improvement comes at a cost. In computer programming, maybe you make your code faster, but this comes at the cost of making the code harder to understand; maybe you are able to remove a lot of dead code, but this comes at the cost of making invasive rearrangements that may introduce bugs; maybe you add a lot of comments making the code easier to understand, but these take up space and make it harder to find what you’re looking for in a pinch. A lot of what goes into making a good computer programmer (and, at a higher level, a good CTO) is the experience to know when some trade-off is worthwhile.

With regards to spirituality, I was granted to be able to hear my angel; the only other person I’ve ever heard of to be similarly gifted is Sokrates, and this is what originally drew me to the Greek tradition as I tried to make sense of it. This has been, of course, a great blessing to me, and has kept me going through otherwise unbearable experiences, and I wouldn’t trade it for anything—but even this comes with tremendous downsides! For example, having experienced divine beauty in a small way, no longer can I appreciate material beauty; having knowledge of the hereafter in a small way, no longer am I fit to live in the here-and-now. Life here is so often boring and painful since my heart and mind are elsewhere! You see the same thing in people who experience NDEs: sometimes, they become more vivacious and joyous, but other times they become utterly dispirited and depressed, longing to return to that wonderful place they visited.

Since humans are almost always supposed to learn to master living as a human, and the direct experience of the divinity is a tremendous hindrance to doing so, this is why the direct experience of divinity is so rare, and why that rarity is a good thing—even as I may wish otherwise!

item.title: 23 Nov 2026
item.description:
καὶ περὶ Ἀγαμήδους δὲ καὶ Τροφωνίου φησὶ Πίνδαρος τὸν νεὼν τὸν ἐν Δελφοῖς οἰκοδομήσαντας αἰτεῖν παρὰ τοῦ Ἀπόλλωνος μισθόν, τὸν δ’ αὐτοῖς ἐπαγγείλασθαι εἰς ἑβδόμην ἡμέραν ἀποδώσειν, ἐν τοσούτῳ δ’ εὐωχεῖσθαι παρακελύσασθαι: τοὺς δὲ ποιήσαντας τὸ προσταχθὲν τῇ ἑβδόμῃ νυκτὶ κατακοιμηθέντας τελευτῆσαι. λέγεται δὲ καὶ αὐτῷ Πινδάρῳ ἐπισκήψαντι τοῖς παρὰ τῶν Βοιωτῶν πεμφθεῖσιν εἰς θεοῦ πυθέσθαι ‘τί ἄριστόν ἐστιν ἀνθρώποις’ ἀποκρίνασθαι τὴν πρόμαντιν ὅτι οὐδ’ αὐτὸς ἀγνοεῖ, εἴ γε τὰ γραφέντα περὶ Τροφωνίου καὶ Ἀγαμήδους ἐκείνου ἐστίν: εἰ δὲ καὶ πειραθῆναι βούλεται, μετ’ οὐ πολὺ ἔσεσθαι αὐτῷ πρόδηλον. καὶ οὕτω πυθόμενον τὸν Πίνδαρον συλλογίζεσθαι τὰ πρὸς τὸν θάνατον, διελθόντος δ’ ὀλίγου χρόνου τελευτῆσαι.

And Pindaros* says that Agamedes and Trophonios,* having built a sanctuary for Apollon in Delphi, asked him for their wages, and he promised to pay them in seven days, but encouraged them meanwhile to enjoy themselves; doing as they were told, they laid down to sleep on the seventh night and died. And it is also said that Pindar himself asked those sent by the Boiotians to consult the god, “what is best for people?” the prophetess replied that he himself ought to know if he wrote the above about Trophonios and Agamedes, but if he also wanted to experience it himself, he wouldn’t have to wait long. And upon learning this, Pindaros concluded that his death was near, and indeed, he died soon after.

  • Pindaros: perhaps the third or fourth most renowned poet of Ancient Greece, after Homeros and Hesiodos and alongside Sappho.
  • Agamedes and Trophonios: ἀγα-μήδεα “very clever” and τροφός “of the Nurse,” the sons of King Erginos of (Boiotian) Orkhomenos (cf. Homeric Hymn III “to Apollon” 294–7).

(Ploutarkhos, Consolation to Apollonios §14.)

item.title: 17 Nov 2026
item.description:
ὧδ’ ἔρδειν· δειλὴν δὲ βροτῶν ὑπαλεύεο φήμην·
φήμη γάρ τε κακὴ πέλεται, κούφη μὲν ἀεῖραι
ῥεῖα μάλ’, ἀργαλέη δὲ φέρειν, χαλεπὴ δ’ ἀποθέσθαι.
φήμη δ’ οὔ τις πάμπαν ἀπόλλυται, ἥντινα πολλοὶ
λαοὶ φημίξουσι: θεός νύ τίς ἐστι καὶ αὐτή.

Act thus and avoid the wretched talk of mortals,
for talk turns trouble: light and easy to pick up,
but heavy to bear and hard to put down.
No talk of anyone dies away whenever many
people speak it, so even it is somehow divine.

(Hesiodos, Works and Days 760–4.)

item.title: 7 Nov 2026
item.description:
I haven’t read him personally to see if it is merited, but Thomas Aquinas is esteemed as the greatest philosopher of the Christian church. One example of this, at least, is that when various groups set out to publish collections of the works which have shaped the Western worldview (e.g. Encyclopædia Britannica’s Great Books of the Western World, whose copies of Euclid and Plotinos sit on my shelf), Aquinas and Dante were the only authors to be collected between the classical world and the Renaissance.

He lectured and wrote voluminously throughout his life. They say that, late in life, Aquinas had an ecstatic experience, after which he refused to write any more. When asked why, he said, “All that I have written seems like straw to me.”

I have not had any ecstatic experiences, but the more I contemplate the mysteries, the more akin I feel to that sentiment. I have often considered simply destroying everything I have written, but that doesn’t seem fair: after all, I have made these notes public as a gift, and it would be graceless to take the gift back...

But please, please take it as the gropings of a student, and trust none of it!

item.title: 2 Nov 2026: Britomartis Appendices
item.description:
Show her how it’s done, Artemis!

Of course, when I said I translated everything from antiquity concerning Britomartis, I meant in Greek. A few things I translated but didn’t include above:

  • Diodoros of Sicily, Library of History V 48–9, 76.3–77.2 (cf. Homeros, Ilias XX 215–240; Hesiodos, Theogoneia 969–74; Homeros, Odusseia V 125–8). (Note that Euboulos “of good counsel” is an epithet of Ploutos “wealthy.”) I didn’t include my translation above because it’s long and almost exclusively about Britomartis’s ancestors—not that this is without interest to the myth! just outside the scope of what I was posting about—though it does note that she was born at Kaino (from καίνω “to kill”).
  • Strabon, Geography X 4.12 is critical of Kallimakhos’s association of Mount Dikte with Diktunna, since the Kudonians (who are said to have raised an altar to her) live in the west of Crete, while Dikte is in the east, doesn’t overlook the sea, and was sacred to Zeus (being his birthplace—Dikte is usually taken to be from τίκτω “to give birth”); he suggests that perhaps Kallimakhos meant Mount Tituros, which is in fact in Kudonia and has a promontory overlooking the sea which was the site of the temple of Diktunna.
  • Various inscriptions engraved on altars, walls, etc. which reference Britomartis, Diktunna, etc. none of which are terribly interesting (except that they often list her alongside Artemis, corroborating accounts that the name refers to a hero in the retinue of Artemis rather than being a mere epithet of her).

I didn’t even look in Latin. This is because I tend to think poorly of Rome and, anyway, can’t read it. I recently found a couple nontrivial Britomartis references in Latin, though:

  • Pseudo-Virgil, Ciris includes Karme (the mother of Britomartis and, as with Antoninos Liberalis, the daughter of Phoinix) as a character and has a digression (283–309) where she laments the loss of her daughter and references the myth. This includes a few details not mentioned or in disagreement with elsewhere: Karme grieves the loss of Britomartis (like Tros of Ganumedes); Britomartis has a Parthian (e.g. recurve composite) bow (like the τόξον παλίντονον of Eurutos, cf. Odusseia XXI 11); Britomartis is punningly associated with δίκταμνον “herb of Dikte” (which we call “dittany of Crete;” cf. Aristoteles, History of Animals IX 7.1; Virgil, Aeneid XII 411–5; Ploutarkhos on the Intelligence of Animals §20); Britomartis is believed to have fallen (rather than leapt) from the promontory into the sea; and Britomartis was said to have hounds (rather than girls) as companions (woof woof).
  • Servius on the Aeneid III 171 briefly recounts the Britomartis myth, calling her Dikte and associating Mount Dikte and dittany with her.

Alas, these don’t meaningfully move the needle on my opinion of Latin sources.
